Short review right here, longer review below: Nothing ever happens. This game NEEDS to be fixed. Not with tamagotchi chicken eggs, not with the random ass crosshair reset from the Sept 22 update, but Valve needs to fix the anti-cheat. Millions of people are quitting this game, blatant cheaters can play multiple ranked games in a row without being VAC-lived, while top-fraggers who don't cheat are falsely cancelled by VACnet on their very first comp match.

[h1]CSGO[/h1]
I bought CSGO in Oct 1, 2014 (CSGO was $30 back then) and played it on and off. I don't have many hours cos of my dookie laptop from a decade ago that couldn't handle CSGO, and also rage quitting when I played on my brother's PC that could run this game lol. This game gave me a gambling addiction as a kid, but I mean that's just every kid who plays this game, not saying I'm special!!! I remember unboxing a gut knife (urban masked FT) and I was so happy, until my account got hacked and the knife was traded off LOL (this happened right before steam implemented 2FA). But my actual gameplay experience was kinda fun, I loved deathmatch and casual, and nobody was toxic until I started playing comp games, where the joke of "Clutch or Kick" was taken VERY literally by silvers. I was kicked because I couldn't clutch a 1v4, and I just gave up on the game for a while. I've played with gold novas who are more chill than most silvers.

[h1]CS2[/h1]
I got back into this game last month, in my opinion CS2 is definitely more beginner-friendly than CSGO. While toxic players are in every competitive game, I've encountered less toxic players here than on CSGO. I LOVE the addition of Follow Recoil, it's very helpful for people trying to learn spray patterns. But CS2 was suggested to me by a friend who was falsely VACnetted on his first comp game of the night (he's 7k premier and silver btw, if you look at his stats he's clearly NOT cheating), wtf happened to manual review of demos like what the Overwatch system did?? What's the point of trying to get better when you're slapped with a 20 hour VAC cooldown for playing good? But the worst part was that I also received the VAC cooldown since I queued with him. CS2's VACnet has produced way more false-flags than CSGO's VAC, and people are saying that the anti-cheat here is better?? HaiX recently put out a video that shows two cheaters playing wingman, and I mean BLATANT hacks like bhopping and jumping headshots with deagles and scouts, and they weren't VAC-lived until the end of their 7th game. The point of an anti-cheat is to detect cheats, not second-hand guess who the cheater is. I don't care how dog💩 I am at CS, I might switch to Faceit if this 💩 keeps happening ([spoiler]which it will lol[/spoiler])

review:
Counter-Strike 2 – A 20+ Year Veteran’s Review

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike since late fall 2002. I fell in love with it immediately and spent weekend after weekend learning the game inside and out. I watched it grow into 1.6 — the version that, for a lot of people my age, still feels like the peak. I put years into it: new teammates, old teammates, LAN events, and countless hours both in and out of my free time because I genuinely loved the game.

When Source came out it was a rough adjustment. I understood that games need to evolve, so I gave it time and eventually got used to it, even while watching the Counter-Strike I originally fell in love with slowly change. Years later, CS:GO arrived. It was nothing like the game I’d known for over a decade, but I kept an open mind and eventually came to enjoy it on its own terms. The problem was that it never stopped changing. Patch after patch, the shift to free-to-play, systems and updates that most long-time players never asked for — the game kept moving further away from what made so many of us fall in love with it in the first place. It felt like it was being slowly buried under its own updates.

CS2 launched and I once again went in with an open mind. What I found was very little meaningful difference from CS:GO. The creative and structural vision that the original Counter-Strike developers had is gone. It feels like the same game is being recycled with a new label, wrapped in more cases, weapon finishes, ranking systems, and monetization layers. At that point I mostly stopped playing regularly. Now I log in maybe once every couple of weeks, sometimes once a month, because it feels like a shell of what I used to know.
I mainly play Dust 2. Because I don’t play often and rarely touch other maps, the ranking system has kept me in Silver for a long time. When I do play I’m usually at the top of the scoreboard. Recently I received a 20-hour VAC cooldown for “irregular gameplay” after using the Scout on Dust 2 during one of the rare days I actually got to play. From what I understand, the new VACNet system is flagging certain movement and weapon usage — including the Scout — as suspicious, even when no cheating is involved.

I’ve known cheaters have been a problem in this series since the beginning. Seeing Valve’s solution start hitting long-time players who simply play the way they’ve always played is a new low. After more than 20 years, this feels like another clear moment where the veteran player base is being pushed further to the side. I’ve been pretty patient with the changes over the years, but getting locked out of the game for a day because I used a Scout on Dust 2 on one of the few times I logged in is a step too far.

I still have a soft spot for Counter-Strike and I’ll probably come back again eventually. But Valve has spent years steadily alienating the players who stuck with the game the longest, and this is one of the clearest examples yet.

and out. i watched it grow into 1.6 — the version that, for a lot of people my age, still feels like the peak. i put years into it: new teammates, old teammates, lan events, and countless hours both in and out of my free time because i genuinely loved the game. when source came out it was a rough adjustment. i understood that games need to evolve, so i gave it time and eventually got used to it, even while watching the counter-strike i originally fell in love with slowly change. years later, cs:go arrived. it was nothing like the game i’d known for over a decade, but i kept an open mind and eventually came to enjoy it on its own terms. the problem was that it never stopped changing. patch after patch, the shift to free-to-play, systems and updates that most long-time players never asked for — the game kept moving further away from what made so many of us fall in love with it in the first place. it felt like it was being slowly buried under its own updates. cs2 launched and i once again went in with an open mind. what i found was very little meaningful difference from cs:go. the creative and structural vision that the original counter-strike developers had is gone. it feels like the same game is being recycled with a new label, wrapped in more cases, weapon finishes, ranking systems, and monetization layers. at that point i mostly stopped playing regularly. now i log in maybe once every couple of weeks, sometimes once a month, because it feels like a shell of what i used to know. i mainly play dust 2. because i don’t play often and rarely touch other maps, the ranking system has kept me in silver for a long time. when i do play i’m usually at the top of the scoreboard. recently i received a 20-hour vac cooldown for “irregular gameplay” after using the scout on dust 2 during one of the rare days i actually got to play. from what i understand, the new vacnet system is flagging certain movement and weapon usage — including the scout — as suspicious, even when no cheating is involved. i’ve known cheaters have been a problem in this series since the beginning. seeing valve’s solution start hitting long-time players who simply play the way they’ve always played is a new low. after more than 20 years, this feels like another clear moment where the veteran player base is being pushed further to the side. i’ve been pretty patient with the changes over the years, but getting locked out of the game for a day because i used a scout on dust 2 on one of the few times i logged in is a step too far. i still have a soft spot for counter-strike and i’ll probably come back again eventually. but valve has spent years steadily alienating the players who stuck with the game the longest, and this is one of the clearest examples yet.

review:
CS2 Is a Disappointing Competitive Shooter: A Detailed Review of Why Counter-Strike 2 Is Bad

An opinionated review of Counter-Strike 2 and why it can feel like a downgrade rather than the next step forward for one of the most iconic competitive shooters ever made.
Introduction: A sequel that doesn't feel like enough of an upgrade

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) had enormous expectations to live up to. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) was one of the most successful competitive shooters of all time, with a legendary esports scene, a dedicated player base, a high skill ceiling, and gameplay that rewarded thousands of hours of practice. When Valve announced CS2, players expected a genuine evolution of the formula: better servers, more consistent hit registration, improved anti-cheat, meaningful quality-of-life improvements, and a polished competitive experience.

Instead, CS2 has often felt like a frustrating mixture of familiar gameplay and persistent technical problems. While the transition to the Source 2 engine brought visual improvements, new smoke mechanics, and updated maps, those changes do not automatically make a game better. A competitive shooter needs to feel responsive, consistent, and fair above everything else.

The biggest criticism of CS2 is that it sometimes feels as though the visual presentation received more attention than the fundamental experience of playing the game. When a player loses a gunfight because of questionable hit registration, encounters a suspected cheater, or experiences inconsistent movement, better lighting and prettier maps provide very little comfort.
1. Inconsistent hit registration and frustrating gunfights

One of the most frustrating aspects of CS2 is the feeling that shots do not always connect in the way players expect them to.

Counter-Strike is built around precision. Every bullet matters, particularly when using weapons such as the AK-47, M4A1-S, or AWP. Players spend hundreds of hours learning recoil patterns, crosshair placement, movement timing, and how to peek angles. In a game with such a high skill ceiling, the shooting mechanics need to feel dependable.

However, some players experience situations where they believe they have landed a clean shot, only for the opponent to survive or kill them almost instantly. Other times, they may die after seemingly reaching cover or feel that an opponent's shot connected despite the visual information on their screen suggesting otherwise.

Not every questionable gunfight is necessarily a technical failure. Counter-Strike relies on server-side hit detection, movement mechanics, recoil, and timing, and players can misjudge what happened. Nevertheless, when the experience repeatedly feels inconsistent, it becomes difficult to trust the game's feedback.

This is particularly damaging because shooting is not a secondary mechanic in CS2. It is the entire foundation of the game. If players cannot confidently understand why they won or lost a duel, the competitive experience becomes significantly less satisfying.

The problem: A precision-based shooter cannot afford to make its core mechanic feel unreliable, regardless of how visually impressive it looks.
2. Sub-tick does not eliminate the feeling of inconsistency

One of CS2's major technical changes was its sub-tick input system. The intention was to improve how the game registers actions such as shooting and movement, rather than relying exclusively on the traditional fixed tick boundaries players associated with CS:GO.

In theory, this should have made the game more responsive and accurate. In practice, however, some players continue to report frustrating discrepancies between what they see and what the game registers.

Peeker's advantage, timing differences, latency, interpolation, and the way movement and shooting are presented can all contribute to these experiences. It would be inaccurate to attribute every frustrating death directly to sub-tick, but the system has not stopped players from questioning the consistency of their gunfights.

For a competitive game, perception matters enormously. Players need to feel that their mechanical skill translates reliably into results. When they repeatedly feel that the game is working against their expectations, they lose confidence in the competitive system.

The criticism is not simply that sub-tick is inherently bad. It is that a major technical overhaul should deliver an unmistakable improvement to the player experience, rather than leave so many players debating whether the fundamentals feel better or worse.
3. Cheating remains a major concern

Cheating is one of the most damaging problems any competitive multiplayer game can face, and CS2 is no exception.

Counter-Strike's competitive structure makes cheating especially frustrating. Matches depend on information gathering, positioning, timing, economy management, and individual mechanical skill. A player who uses wallhacks, aim assistance, or other prohibited software can undermine all of those systems at once.

Imagine spending thirty minutes carefully coordinating with teammates, managing your economy, and adapting to the enemy's strategies, only to suspect that an opponent has an unfair advantage. Even if the match is technically winnable, the experience becomes less about strategy and more about questioning whether the competition is legitimate.

The existence of cheating in a game does not automatically mean its developers are doing nothing to combat it. Anti-cheat is an ongoing challenge, and suspicious behavior can sometimes have legitimate explanations. Nevertheless, the perceived prevalence of cheaters can be enough to undermine trust in ranked matchmaking.

Valve's approach to anti-cheat and enforcement has long been a subject of debate among players. When players do not understand how suspicious accounts are detected, how reports are handled, or whether repeat offenders are being removed effectively, confidence in the system suffers.

The problem: Competitive integrity is not an optional feature. If players cannot trust that their opponents are competing fairly, ranks and match victories lose some of their meaning.
4. Matchmaking can be an exhausting experience

CS2's matchmaking can feel less like a competitive environment designed to produce satisfying games and more like a repeated test of patience.

A good matchmaking system should create reasonably balanced matches, account for individual performance over time, and encourage players to improve. In reality, competitive matches can sometimes feel extremely uneven, with large differences in individual skill, teamwork, communication, and experience.

One match may feature coordinated teams that communicate effectively and understand their roles. The next may involve teammates who refuse to cooperate, players who leave early, arguments over minor mistakes, or individuals who give up after losing a few rounds.

Some of this is unavoidable in a team-based game. No matchmaking algorithm can guarantee perfect teammates or eliminate differences in player behavior. But that does not make the experience less frustrating.

The ranking system can also feel discouraging when players struggle to understand their progress. Losing several games in a row can make improvement feel meaningless, particularly when individual performance does not translate into victories.

And because CS2 places so much emphasis on teamwork, one player's mistakes can have a disproportionate impact on an entire match. You can practice your aim, learn utility lineups, improve your positioning, and still lose because your team repeatedly makes poor decisions.

The result is a competitive experience that can feel punishing without always feeling rewarding.
5. Toxicity makes the community difficult to enjoy.
